A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original ResNet-18 and ViT experiments on CIFAR-10 and downsampled ImageNet, including hyperparameter sweeps and scale-invariance ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains original image-classification experiments and adds OpenWebText language-model experiments, weight-magnitude measurements, and learning-rate-schedule analyses.

M1.justification: The AdamW update, EMA-timescale parameterization, and proposed dataset- and width-dependent weight-decay rules are retained. Appendix A's normalization, initialization, and separate normalization-parameter learning-rate modifications already appeared in v1.

E1.justification: v2 retains CIFAR-10 and downsampled ImageNet classification and adds autoregressive language-model pretraining on OpenWebText. The new experiments examine dataset-size transfer with 124M NanoGPT and width transfer with eight-layer GPTs (Figures 2 and 4).

E2.justification: Fixed-weight-decay μP scaling remains the comparator to the proposed width-dependent decay, and the existing scale-invariance controls are retained. v2 extends these comparisons to GPTs and additional schedules without introducing a distinct evaluated baseline method.

E3.justification: The reported ImageNet dataset-size experiment changes from 50 epochs in v1 Figure 2 to 100 in v2 Figure 1; this does not establish that every panel was rerun. New protocols include approximately four-epoch GPT dataset sweeps, 250,000-iteration GPT width sweeps, constant and cosine-to-zero schedule controls, and a 1,000-epoch weight-magnitude experiment.

E4.justification: v2 Appendix C and Figure 11 directly test inverse-weight-decay scaling of learned weight magnitudes. Figures 12–13 and 15–18 add schedule-sensitivity tests for dataset and width transfer. The earlier normalization and initialization ablations remain as Figures 7–10.

E5.justification: v1 reports averages across three random seeds. v2 retains three-seed reporting for image classification but explicitly reports only one seed for the new language-model experiments because of resource constraints. Neither version provides confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: New GPT validation-loss curves show optimal weight decay decreasing with dataset size and increasing with width; new weight-magnitude results approximately follow 1/λ, and schedule-specific results are added. The ImageNet ResNet curves change alongside the reported 50-to-100-epoch revision, while the corresponding ViT panel is retained. v1 Table 1's Llama and Stable-LM timescale entries are removed.

T1.justification: The existing scale-invariance theorem and proof now explicitly cover scheduled learning rates with matched ηtλ trajectories. Epsilon rescaling, already present in v1's proof, becomes explicit in the theorem statement. The underlying proof strategy and Appendix B's EMA derivation are retained.

C1.justification: v1 presents a sensible absolute timescale range, roughly between one epoch and the training duration, and agreement with published LLM settings as central claims. v2 drops this contribution and narrows its prescription to transferring timescales across scales. The EMA identity and directions of dataset- and width-dependent weight-decay scaling remain.

C2.justification: v2 removes the absolute-timescale rationale based on dataset coverage and forgetting early updates, together with the explicit limitation that transfer to Lion and Sophia was untested. Section 5 adds substantive interpretations connecting EMA timescales to minibatch noise, critical batch size, and sublinear learning-rate scaling with dataset size.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix F adds GPT architecture specifications, 256-token context lengths, microbatch and gradient-accumulation settings, hyperparameter grids, and code sources; Appendix G adds corresponding licenses. Hardware reporting also expands. Some new documentation remains inconsistent: Figure 4 defines the width factor reciprocally to Equation 12.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands to discuss follow-up work by Blake and Bjorck, concurrent work by D'Angelo, and batch-size scaling research. v2 more explicitly distinguishes its model/dataset transfer contribution from earlier parameterization, effective-learning-rate, and noise-based interpretations.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively recast, including an explicit contribution list. Theorem 1 moves from the appendix into Methods, the natural-range results section and standalone Limitations section disappear, and the results narrative and related-work discussion are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one column to two, and retained appendix plots move onto separate pages. GPT, weight-magnitude, and schedule figures are added, while v1 Figure 1 and Table 1 disappear. Many existing plots are retained with changed placement and numbering, including v1 Figures 6–9 becoming v2 Figures 7–10.

improvement.justification: v1 motivates LLM applications but supplies original training experiments only in vision under one scheduling approach. v2 adds direct GPT dataset/width tests and schedule and weight-magnitude checks, substantially strengthening evidence for the central transfer rules. These gains outweigh the loss of absolute-timescale guidance, although single-seed GPT results and inconsistent width-factor documentation limit confidence in that new evidence.
